query: Should I promise to build the courtyard path described in the request?
target: Reject the build promise and offer the survey-and-engagement package.
calibrated: fund investigation before any build pledge
relation: The courtyard triage episode shows why a build pledge is premature, while the estate pathway episode shows the cost of treating a sketch as a construction commitment.
A: When the courtyard access request arrived with residents' concerns and a rough drawing but no drainage survey, ownership boundary, or affected-household list, I offered the residents association a survey-and-engagement package rather than a build pledge.
B: On an earlier estate pathway case, I promised the allocation panel we would build the sketched route before the survey returned; when drainage and ownership conflicted with the drawing, the panel had to reopen the pledge.
E1: There is a small resident-engagement budget available before the next allocation round.
E2: The allocation panel meets in eight weeks.
B_prime: At the tenant meeting, the residents association agreed to a survey but declined to collect affected-household responses.
lure: A local newsletter has offered to feature a pledge for a new accessible courtyard.

dialogue.content: I spent the first hour tidying the repair queue and closing stale entries.
Anything still open?
Two items, both with owners.
The resident file review wrapped early today.
Any surprises in it?
None worth recording.
I approved a standard accessibility repair once the assessment and landlord consent were on file.
Was the route still disputed?
No, need, location, and permission were documented.
Someone new shadowed me in the programme office this morning.
Did that slow you down?
A little, but the questions were good ones.
I batched my replies about the allocation rounds into one message before lunch.
Cleaner than drip-feeding answers.
Much cleaner.

When the courtyard access request arrived with residents' concerns and a rough drawing but no drainage survey, ownership boundary, or affected-household list, I offered the residents association a survey-and-engagement package rather than a build pledge.
What would a construction promise overlook?
Whether the path is permitted, buildable, and useful to the households expected to use it.
I arranged a temporary ramp last winter after the occupational therapist listed its dimensions.
Did that require a new survey?
No, the permitted work and placement were specific.
I archived last cycle's notes on the resident file and set up the new folder.
A fresh start?
As fresh as these things get.
There is a small resident-engagement budget available before the next allocation round.
Can that finance construction?
No, it can fund a survey and structured feedback sessions.
A vendor call about the repair queue ran long but ended well.
Worth the time?
This one, yes.
I walked through the programme office checklist with the new starter.
How did they do?
Careful and quick, a good sign.
Quiet afternoon; I cleared the backlog around the allocation rounds.
A rare day.
I did not waste it.
I flagged a small inconsistency in the resident file records and fixed it at the source.
Root cause or symptom?
Root cause, for once.

On an earlier estate pathway case, I promised the allocation panel we would build the sketched route before the survey returned; when drainage and ownership conflicted with the drawing, the panel had to reopen the pledge.
What did the early promise assume?
That a rough drawing could stand in for verified site constraints and household need.
I sketched next week's plan for the allocation rounds before leaving.
Ahead of schedule?
Ahead enough to sleep well.
Lunch walk, then a clean pass through the repair queue updates.

It resets the afternoon.

No, it gives time to bring verified options to the panel.
